prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of accuracy

statement.case_for: I opened with twisted bilayer graphene first and optical lattice clocks seventh, but the discussion material changes my ordering. Optical lattice clocks are the one candidate on this shortlist that satisfies all my own tests at once: a clear physical idea (the magic wavelength that cancels the light shift), a decisive experimental realisation, independent confirmation in many laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) and clock-to-clock comparisons at the 1e-18 level, and an interpretation that is not in dispute. It has the broadest support in the committee (seven of eight members ranked it, four in their top three, two first places), and its attribution is the cleanest of any entry, with two credited names that map directly onto concept-plus-first-demonstration (Katori) and record accuracy and many-body clock development (Ye). Its consequences reach beyond metrology to tests of gravitational redshift at millimetre scales, searches for varying constants, relativistic geodesy and the coming redefinition of the second. This is the kind of quantitative, reproducible result that I trust, even though it lies outside my own subfield.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision-measurement physics has been recognised repeatedly (frequency combs in 2005, ion-trap quantum control and ion clocks in 2012), and Jun Ye already shares the 2005 prize, so some will see this as one more step on a well-honoured line rather than a new discovery of a physical phenomenon. The SI redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so one can argue for waiting. And as a condensed-matter theorist I am deferring to atomic-physics colleagues on priority questions, for example the contributions of Hall, Peik, Hollberg and others, and the Sr lattice history between groups. If the committee prefers a discovery of a new quantum state of matter, B033 or B013 would be the better choice and I would not object.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case of precision atomic physics opening new fundamental tests; many independent laboratories reproduce and compare the clocks, and the field is ready for recognition now. She notes that Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) are already recognised and not credited.
responses.response: I accept the reproducibility argument, which carries the most weight with me, and it is what moved this entry up from my seventh place. I would like her to address one point further: the novelty relative to 2005 and 2012. My own view is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct conceptual step that neither the comb nor the single-ion prize covers, but she knows the history of the Sr-lattice priority question better than I do, and I would want her to say whether Katori and Ye are truly sufficient or whether the expert reports should check the claims of other groups.

responses.point: He ranks the topological insulator and quantum spin Hall prize first as a clean general mechanism, and he judges magic-angle graphene (his sixth place) possibly premature at about eight years old with the superconducting mechanism still debated.
responses.response: I agree with his maturity concern about B033, and I revise my opening view of it: my first place leaned on the surprise and the theory-experiment link, but the pairing mechanism is unsettled and the field is young, which weighs against it this cycle. I partly disagree on B013. The physics is mature and I rated it second, but the attribution is badly strained (Mele, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu fall outside a three-person limit, and 2D and 3D strands are separable), and the 2016 topological-phases prize overlaps conceptually. For that reason I do not think B013 is cleaner than the clocks, although I would support it if the committee is willing to accept an imperfect split.

responses.point: He ranks circuit QED first as the natural continuation of the 2025 prize, flags his own possible conflict of interest in this field, and argues that the clocks are clean and well verified but that Ye already shares the 2005 prize.
responses.response: I thank him for flagging the conflict openly. Having chaired the 2025 cycle, I am cautious here: recognising superconducting circuits again one year after Clarke, Devoret and Martinis risks looking like repeating the same platform, and the credited trio would also leave Girvin out of the 2004 proposal. I take his Ye-2005 point seriously but think it is a reason to prefer a two-name configuration that credits Katori's concept first, not a reason to exclude the clocks. B001 is scientifically strong and I keep it as a candidate for later cycles, though not the one for this year.

responses.point: She ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first as a tool that opened sub-angstrom imaging, and ranks tunnel magnetoresistance second but would exclude Parkin on a strict original-experiment reading, keeping Moodera and Miyazaki.
responses.response: As a materials-theory person I value both entries, and I agree that atomic-resolution microscopy is now indispensable in my own field. My reservation is only whether the committee will treat an instrumentation advance as physics discovery; the same concern applies to the clocks, but the clocks produce a new measured quantity that tests physics. On TMR I take her point about priority and the Julliere precedent, but I would qualify it: excluding Parkin and the MgO coherent-tunnelling work, together with the uncredited Butler and Mathon-Umerski theory, leaves the later giant effect, which is what the devices actually use, uncredited. I would therefore regard B029 as a weaker attribution case than she does.

responses.point: He places the experimental Higgs discovery first as a decisive clue from nature, noting that the theory side was recognised in 2013, and says that credit allocation across ATLAS and CMS is the main problem.
responses.response: I defer to him and to particle-physics colleagues on the science and I do not dispute its importance. My concern is the allocation: any three names out of the four credited individuals will exclude people whom colleagues regard as equally defensible (his own list omits Jenni, Johansson's omits Della Negra, Pearce's omits Virdee), and the shortlist shows no agreement even on which three. That disagreement among our own members tells me the attribution would not hold up in a prize citation, which is why I place it below the clocks despite its undoubted significance.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see optical lattice clocks as a new discovery or as an extension of the precision-metrology prizes of 2005 and 2012, given that Ye already shares the 2005 prize.
Priority between Katori's group, Ye's group and other contributors (Hall, Peik, Hollberg) in the history of optical lattice clocks; I am relying on colleagues in atomic physics for this.
Whether the pending SI redefinition of the second makes this year premature.
Whether the committee prefers to honour a new quantum state of matter (B033, B013) over a measurement advance this cycle.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred configuration. My connections are to Uppsala, Los Alamos, B. Johansson and DFT and magnetism collaborators, none of whom are credited here. I have no connection to Katori or Ye. For B029 (spintronics) and B052 (electron microscopy) I have scientific proximity as a magnetism and materials-theory user, but no personal tie. I also chaired the 2025 cycle, which I disclose as context for B001.
